Round three Chunk Boundary Ablation: complete-pipeline supplementary report

# Round three Chunk Boundary Ablation: complete-pipeline supplementary report

Named at the user's request; the internal execution directories remain round4/round4_full_20261030 so that renaming does not break the evidence. Report generated: 2026-10-30T03:51:03.902510+00:00. Original time window 02:11:08–04:11:08 UTC, not reset because of the environment diagnosis or the resumed run.

**Actually added: 18/18 independent indexes; mix natural queries 18/18, naive natural queries 18/18, forced original-text diagnostics 18/18.**
3 groups of complete original index documents, each with same-chunk A / cross-chunk B × 3 runs. The old minimal extraction control on claims 1/27 is kept and not repeated; the independent environment-recovery smoke test is not counted in these ablation results.

The pre-frozen technical core of all 36 natural answers passed the check against the original text, but it cannot be said that all answers are completely correct: the naive answer of F01_B_r2 invented a claim-dependency chain, and in several answers the text inside quotation marks is not strictly verbatim. Main finding: F01 shows a boundary-sensitive **omission of a predicate from the explicit relation records**, first visible in the raw extraction, while original-text retrieval and the core answer still succeed. In F05 and F04 the target component predicates are kept in the verified A/B results. This must not be interpreted as crossing chunks generally causing knowledge loss; F01 has only one pair without truncation, and the other groups also differ in chunk count and amount of repeated tokens.

F01 — US9589231B2

In US9589231B2, how are the existing medical cases and the set of experts embedded with respect to an ontology, and what named terminology system underlies that ontology? Identify the supporting claims and distinguish the explicit technical chain from an inferred shortcut relation.

```
4. The method of claim 1 , wherein the embedding of the new medical case in the embedding space comprises computing a multidimensional representation of the medical case based on a medical ontology, the embedding of the existing medical cases and the set of experts being also based on the medical ontology.

8. The method of claim 4 , wherein the medical ontology is based on the Unified Medical Language System.
```

## D. The two most valuable cases

### Success: US8069128B2, claims 6 and 10

Claim 10: “wherein the multi-pass message filter employs a Naive Bayes classifier.” Claim 6: “the second classification data is configured to reside exclusively in a non-persistent memory store”. A and B 3 runs each without truncation; the use of the classifier, the generation of the data, the non-persistent memory and the “exclusively” limitation all enter the raw relation records and the merged graph, and mix natural retrieval also returns claims 6/10 and correctly distinguishes the persistent data of the first filter.

For example, the actual relations and source_ids of F05_B_r1 can be checked in merged_graph.json. In condition A, NaiveBayes connects to “Multi-Pass Ad-Hoc Spam Message Filter”, while SecondClassificationData connects to “Multi-Pass Message Filter”; there is also an alternative ClassificationModel path supported by the text. The report separates the actual same-ID chain from the retention of the semantic fact; it neither judges a dedup defect from naming differences alone nor adds alias edges artificially.

### A locatable omission: US9589231B2, F01_A_r3 / F01_B_r3

Claim 4 explicitly contains “the embedding of the existing medical cases and the set of experts being also based on the medical ontology”; claim 8 explicitly states “the medical ontology is based on the Unified Medical Language System”. Both runs are without truncation: the same full text, the same 2 chunk extractions, the same 1819 processed source tokens; only the boundary and the length split differ.

A3's raw relation output contains the following two records; the description of the first keeps both the cases and the experts predicate. **They are not three direct endpoint edges**:

```
relation<|#|>Diagnosis Assistance Method<|#|>Medical Ontology<|#|>embeds based on<|#|>The embedding of the new medical case, existing medical cases, and experts is based on a medical ontology.
relation<|#|>Medical Ontology<|#|>Unified Medical Language System<|#|>based on<|#|>The medical ontology is based on the Unified Medical Language System.
```

B3's raw relation output has no explicit ontology-basis predicate for existing cases or experts; the UMLS predicate is kept. Parsing and merging cause no additional loss of these targets, so the earliest visible stage is **the relation representation of the extraction**. B's entity descriptions still keep part of the general medical-case/expert meaning, so it cannot be said that all knowledge disappeared.

A1/A2 also show the predicate kept, but both hit the 3500 output cap; all three B runs lack the predicate and have no truncation. The overall observation A 3/3, B 0/3 must be shown together with the truncation information; the only clean pair is r3. In particular, the claim 4 relation sentence exists complete inside B's first chunk, so this cannot show that “a relation that can only be understood by joining two chunks was cut”. More accurately: under this group's boundary and context rearrangement, the explicit relation representation is unstable.

All F01 mix queries retrieved both original passages and answered claims 4/8 and UMLS correctly, and the forced original-text diagnostics succeeded too. “The answer is correct” and “the predicate is complete in the graph” therefore come apart here; original-text retrieval can compensate for omissions in the graph representation. Evidence paths: parsed_extraction.json, merged_graph.json, chunks.json and natural_query.json in results/F01_A_r3 and F01_B_r3, and the corresponding logs/api_* requests and responses.

### Another clear generation error: the claim dependency of F01_B_r2 naive

The naive answer writes claim 4 → claim 5 → claim 6 → claim 8 as “the stated sequence of dependencies”. Claim 8 actually begins “The method of claim 4” and depends directly on claim 4; natural retrieval had returned the complete original text. This additional dependency-chain error can therefore be located at the generation stage and cannot be blamed on missing text or a retrieval omission. The technical core is still correct, so a score of technical QA alone would miss this error.

### Listed separately: format and faithfulness of explanations

The last relation line of F01_A_r2 is incomplete because of output truncation; F04_B_r2 has 3 non-target relations with missing fields, so the 20 raw lines yield only 17 parsed relations. This is an actual schema rejection; the target cost predicate is kept, and no parser algorithm error can be asserted from it.

The natural answer of F04_A_r1 additionally calls claims 12/13 alternative parameters and the cost only one option. The original claims make no explicit statement of alternatives; the raw SpecifiedParameter entity summary already contains an “or”-type generalisation, and the answer interprets it further. It is marked as a warning about the faithfulness of the explanation; the exact causal propagation cannot be attributed uniquely, and it is not treated as a confirmed chunk failure or a legal conclusion.

## E. Research judgments

| Question | Judgment supported by this experiment |
| ---|--- |
| Document-level provenance | The current v1.5.7 returns actual file_paths and references; the correct publication number of this small corpus can be traced. The reliability of competitive retrieval across many patents cannot be inferred from single-target-document indexes. |
| Claim-level provenance | When the original claims keep their numbers and are retrieved, core claim location works well, but F01_B2 naive still generated a wrong dependency chain with complete evidence; the default graph does not guarantee an explicit claim-dependency structure, citations are mostly document mappings, and verbatim quotes do not all match strictly. Linking claim-span evidence to graph assertions needs separate verification. |
| Cross-chunk relation loss | A boundary-sensitive omission of a relation-record predicate was observed in F01; there is only 1 clean pair, and the omitted predicate itself was not cut. No loss of target component predicates was observed in F05/F04. It cannot be claimed that crossing chunks generally causes knowledge loss. |
| Stage of failure | The additional claim-dependency error of F01_B2 naive is earliest at the generation stage; the F01 target omission is earliest in the raw extracted relation output, and an additional parser/merge loss of the target can be ruled out; original-text retrieval still succeeds. Truncation is a condition of this run's output budget. Non-target schema rejections, rewritten quotes and the explanatory warning are listed separately; where attribution is not unique, no stage is forced. |
| Code defect or design limitation | No LightRAG core code defect was confirmed by this experiment. The results rather support research topics around the context sensitivity of LLM extraction representations, the default ontology not enforcing claim structure, the granularity of entity naming, and citation constraints in generation; the limitations of the current configuration and the small sample apply as well. |
| Directions worth pursuing | Assertion-level provenance: link every technical predicate to the original claim/character span; extraction stability and uncertainty; consistency between graph representation and original-text retrieval; auditable merging of aliases and actual graph connectivity; diagnosing “answer correct but graph incomplete” with process measures. |

Every source_id must be interpreted together with run_id/workspace and the chunk hash: different independent indexes can produce the same “publication number-chunk-000” while their boundaries/content differ. Copying a source_id on its own loses the experimental scope. Source ID strings are not used as global evidence identifiers across indexes.
